transcript: Our small team was repeatedly restoring the wrong version of a background worker during incidents. The deployment dashboard showed several similar build names, and the existing instructions assumed that everyone remembered which queue each worker served. During one incident I watched an experienced colleague follow the page correctly and still restart the wrong service. I treated that as a documentation problem rather than an individual mistake. I owned the replacement runbook and first walked through the task with someone who had never performed it. I wrote down the decisions they had to make, added a short check of the queue name before any command, and included the expected output after each step. I separated diagnosis from recovery and added a clear stop point when the observed output did not match. I also put the rollback command beside the deployment command so it was available under pressure. Before publishing, I tested the instructions in a staging environment and asked two teammates to complete the exercise without my help. Their questions showed that one screenshot concealed an important environment label, so I replaced it with a text example. Over the next six weeks, the median recovery exercise fell from eighteen minutes to seven, and nobody selected the wrong worker. The useful part was not the length of the document. It was that each action had a visible check and a safe next step.

I would start with examples of the actual product task rather than a general leaderboard. For a support drafting feature, I would collect a set of fictional messages covering common requests, missing information and cases where the model should decline to guess. I would run both models with the same instructions and compare the drafts against a short checklist. The checklist would include whether the answer addresses the request, whether it invents facts and whether a person could use it with a small edit. I would also measure response time and the cost per draft, because a slightly better answer might not justify a much slower experience. I would ask another person to review some outputs without knowing which model produced them. Then I would choose the model that fits the product requirements and test it on more examples. I have not yet decided how many examples would be enough or what difference would count as meaningful. I would probably begin with the cheaper model if the results looked similar, while keeping the option to change it later.

I would make a page where you can paste a link and give it a title. There would be a list of the links and a box at the top for searching them. Tags would be useful because people could group their bookmarks by topic. I think a relational database would work, although I would need to look into exactly how the tables should be arranged. The interface should be simple and show the most recent bookmarks first. You could click a tag to see matching links, and perhaps change the title after saving. For search, I would initially try matching the text that the user typed against the title. There are probably issues with duplicate links and links that stop working, but I would leave those until later. I would also want the app to work on a phone. I have not thought through signing in, keeping different users separate or what should happen if a save request fails. Those details would need more design before implementation.
